# Pixtega

Pixtega is an on-demand image derivation service, written in Rust. It fetches
an image from an operator-configured source (HTTP(S), filesystem, or S3),
derives a bounded variant (width, format, optional quality), and returns
cacheable image bytes. The Rust crate and binary are also named `pixtega`.
MIT licensed.

This file is the full public documentation of https://pixtega.com as one
Markdown document, for agents and LLMs. A short curated index is at
https://pixtega.com/llms.txt. The canonical sources are the HTML pages under
https://pixtega.com and the repository README at
https://github.com/kroofy/Pixtega/blob/main/README.md.

---

Source: https://pixtega.com/ and https://github.com/kroofy/Pixtega/blob/main/README.md

## Overview

Pixtega resizes and re-encodes images when they're requested. WebP, AVIF,
JPEG. It returns bytes a CDN can cache hard. Keep the original. Pixtega
builds the sizes you allow. No asset-pipeline ritual.

### One URL per image

Anatomy of a Pixtega URL:

```text
GET /images            <- prefix (path_prefix, default "/images")
    /public            <- mount
    /photos/example.jpg <- source path
    /w1280.webp        <- transform: width + format
    ?v=7d91c2          <- optional version token
```

The mount (`public`) picks a configured source. The path names the original.
The last segment is the size and format: `w{width}[,q{quality}].{format}`.
Widths and qualities come from allowlists. An optional `v` query param is for
cache busting when the original changes.

### What a URL gives you

Store one original. Every variant is the same URL with a different final
segment — and only allowlisted widths and qualities exist. For one stored
original `photos/example.jpg` (4000×3000), with the values from
`config.example.toml` (widths `[320, 640, 1280, 1920]`, per-format quality
allowlists):

- `/w1280.webp` → 1280×960 WebP, quality 82 (the WebP default)
- `/w640.avif` → 640×480 AVIF, quality 55 (the AVIF default)
- `/w320,q70.jpeg` → 320×240 JPEG, quality 70 (from the allowlist)
- `/w2000.webp` → 400 Bad Request (2000 is not an allowed width)

Successes are CDN-cacheable; errors are `no-store`.

### Why Pixtega

- **Keep the original.** You store one file. When a size is requested,
  Pixtega builds it. No export script. No folder of thumbnails to keep in
  sync.
- **You allow the sizes.** Widths, formats, and qualities are allowlists in
  the config. A caller cannot invent a 10,000px request. The service never
  upscales.
- **One URL per image.** Same original, same size, same format: same path.
  Put it on a page and leave it.
- **Built to sit behind a CDN.** Successes come back with Cache-Control a
  CDN can honor. Errors are no-store, so a failed request does not poison
  the cache.
- **Sources stay behind mount names.** HTTP, the filesystem, or S3. Callers
  see a mount name. Never a hostname, a bucket, or a directory.
- **Honest errors. Quiet logs.** Permission denied is a 502, not a cacheable
  404. One structured JSON line per request. Credentials stay out of the
  log.
- **Small to run.** One Rust binary or a Lambda image. TOML config. Encoders
  are checked at startup, so a missing format fails the deploy instead of
  the request.

### Output formats

WebP, AVIF, and JPEG, each with its own default quality and quality
allowlist. Encoding uses libvips. Every enabled encoder is checked at
startup. A deploy missing an encoder fails then, not when the first request
asks for that format.

---

Source: https://pixtega.com/docs/getting-started.html

## Getting started

Pixtega ships as a single Rust binary named `pixtega`. Run it locally with
cargo or in a container — the repository bundles fixture images so the quick
start needs no network access.

### Quick start (bundled fixtures, no network)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kroofy/Pixtega.git
cd Pixtega
cargo run -- config.local.toml
# in another shell:
curl -o out.webp 'http://127.0.0.1:8080/images/fixtures/photos/example.jpg/w640.webp'
```

`config.local.toml` serves the bundled `fixtures/` directory through a
filesystem source mounted at `fixtures`. The response is a 640-pixel-wide
WebP derived from the bundled JPEG.

### Build dependencies

The service encodes with libvips, so building from source needs the libvips
development headers.

#### Linux (Debian/Ubuntu)

```bash
sudo apt-get install libvips-dev libheif-plugin-aomenc pkg-config
cargo run -- config.local.toml
```

Ubuntu splits libheif encoders into plugin packages. Without
`libheif-plugin-aomenc`, AVIF encoding is unavailable and the service
refuses to start when `[formats.avif]` is enabled — it verifies every
enabled encoder at startup.

The pinned libvips bindings (`=2.3.0`) pass argument names introduced in
libvips 8.17, so older distribution packages (e.g. Ubuntu 24.04's libvips
8.15) fail at runtime; libvips 8.17+ is required (Ubuntu 26.04+).

#### macOS

```bash
brew install vips pkg-config
cargo run -- config.local.toml
```

Homebrew's `vips` includes AVIF support via libheif.

### Docker

```bash
docker build -t pixtega .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 pixtega            # serves config.example.toml
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 \
  -v "$PWD/myconfig.toml:/config/config.toml:ro" \
  pixtega /config/config.toml
```

The image's default command serves `config.example.toml`, which listens on
`0.0.0.0:8080` and includes the bundled fixtures mount. Pass your own TOML
path as the container command to replace it.

### Next steps

- Configuration (https://pixtega.com/docs/configuration.html) — the full
  TOML schema, precedence, and validation rules.
- API reference (https://pixtega.com/docs/api.html) — URL grammar, caching,
  and the error taxonomy.
- Deploy on AWS Lambda (https://pixtega.com/docs/aws-lambda.html) — the
  recommended serverless deployment path.

---

Source: https://pixtega.com/docs/configuration.html

## Configuration

Pixtega is configured with a single TOML document. The schema is closed: an
unknown field stops startup, as does any invalid value. There are no silent
defaults for limits — what you configure is what runs.

### Where configuration comes from

The service checks three places, in this order, and uses the first match:

1. **CLI argument** — a TOML file path passed as the first argument:
   `pixtega /path/to/config.toml`
2. **`CONFIG_FILE`** — an environment variable holding a TOML file path.
3. **`CONFIG`** — an environment variable holding the full TOML document
   inline. Useful where mounting files is awkward, such as AWS Lambda.

If none is provided, startup fails with
`no configuration: pass a TOML path, or set CONFIG_FILE or CONFIG`.
Relative paths inside a config file (filesystem roots, CA certificate
files) resolve against the file's directory; with inline `CONFIG`, they
resolve against the process working directory.

### Annotated overview

This mirrors `config.example.toml` from the repository
(https://github.com/kroofy/Pixtega/blob/main/config.example.toml):

```toml
# Where to listen.
listen_address = "0.0.0.0:8080"
# URL prefix for the image contract; requests outside it are rejected.
path_prefix = "/images"

# The closed Width Allowlist. Callers may only request these widths.
allowed_widths = [320, 640, 1280, 1920]

# Source size cap (bytes), enforced on the advertised length and again
# while streaming.
max_download_bytes = 52428800
# Decode-bomb guard, checked from header metadata before decoding.
max_source_megapixels = 100
# One timeout over the whole source exchange.
download_timeout_ms = 10000
# Whole-request deadline. Waiting for a max_concurrent_derivations
# permit, the source fetch (download_timeout_ms, which must not exceed
# this), and image processing all spend from this one budget; expiry is
# a non-cacheable 504, possibly before the fetch or processing even
# starts. Optional; defaults to 9000. Keep it below any host kill
# deadline (e.g. an AWS Lambda function timeout).
request_timeout_ms = 30000
# HTTP(S) redirect bound (same origin, same base path only).
max_redirects = 3
# Process-wide fetch+process permits.
max_concurrent_derivations = 8
# Cache lifetime of 200 responses without a `v` token.
unversioned_success_ttl_seconds = 3600
# Cache lifetime of 404 responses.
not_found_ttl_seconds = 60

# How the `v` query parameter is treated. Optional; defaults to "accept".
#   accept - a valid `v` upgrades the response to immutable caching
#   ignore - `v` is validated as usual but the response is served with
#            unversioned_success_ttl_seconds, as if no `v` were present
#   reject - any `v` is a 400 (for deployments that version by path)
version_token = "accept"

# One block per enabled output format. `default_quality` is required.
# An empty or absent `allowed_qualities` means callers cannot pass `q`
# for that format at all.
[formats.webp]
default_quality = 82
allowed_qualities = [60, 72, 90]

[formats.avif]
default_quality = 55
allowed_qualities = [40, 65]

[formats.jpeg]
default_quality = 85
allowed_qualities = [70, 92]

# Each source maps a mount name to a backend. Callers can never supply
# a hostname, bucket, directory, or transport — only the mount.
[[sources]]
mount = "public"          # [a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}, unique
key_prefix = "media"      # omitted => defaults to the mount; "" => none
transport = "http"        # or "filesystem" or "s3"
base_url = "https://images.example.test"

[[sources]]
mount = "fixtures"
key_prefix = ""
transport = "filesystem"
root = "./fixtures"       # resolved relative to the config file

[[sources]]
mount = "archive"
key_prefix = "originals"
transport = "s3"
bucket = "example-image-bucket"
region = "us-east-1"
```

### Limits and allowed ranges

| Field | Range | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allowed_widths` | each in 1..=16384 | the closed Width Allowlist |
| `max_download_bytes` | 1..=104857600 | source size cap, enforced on the advertised length and again while streaming |
| `max_source_megapixels` | 1..=500 | decode-bomb guard, checked from header metadata before decoding |
| `download_timeout_ms` | 1..=60000 | one timeout over the whole source exchange; never larger than `request_timeout_ms` |
| `request_timeout_ms` | 1..=300000 | whole-request deadline (optional, default 9000); permit wait, fetch, and processing spend from this one budget, expiry is a non-cacheable 504 |
| `max_redirects` | 0..=10 | HTTP(S) redirect bound (same origin, same base path only) |
| `max_concurrent_derivations` | 1..=64 | process-wide fetch+process permits |
| `unversioned_success_ttl_seconds` | 1..=86400 | cache lifetime without `v` |
| `not_found_ttl_seconds` | 1..=3600 | cache lifetime of 404s |
| `version_token` | `accept` \| `ignore` \| `reject` | what the `v` query parameter means (default `accept`; any other value stops startup) |

`request_timeout_ms` is the deadline for answering one request: waiting for
a `max_concurrent_derivations` permit, the source fetch (bounded by
`download_timeout_ms`, which must not exceed it), and decode/resize/encode
all spend from the same budget, and expiry is a real 504 with
`Cache-Control: no-store` — a request queued behind slow derivations can
therefore time out before its fetch or processing even starts. Keep the
deadline below any host kill deadline
(for example an AWS Lambda function timeout) so the service answers before
the host tears the response down mid-stream. A timed-out encode cannot be
cancelled: it keeps occupying its `max_concurrent_derivations` slot until
libvips returns.

`version_token` is the operator lever over the `v` cache-busting parameter:
`accept` (the default) lets a valid `v` upgrade the response to year-long
immutable caching; `ignore` validates the same grammar but serves the
response with `unversioned_success_ttl_seconds` as if no `v` were present;
`reject` turns any `v` into a 400, like any other unknown query parameter —
useful when sources are versioned by path. A missing `v` is fine in every
mode.

### Source transports

#### http

Requires `base_url` (http or https). An optional `ca_certificate_file`
(PEM, HTTPS only, resolved relative to the config file) supports local
fixture servers; hostname verification always stays on. Use HTTPS outside
loopback and trusted private networks; plain http is intended for local
fixtures and trusted internal hops only.

Pin `base_url` to an origin you control. A destination policy is enforced
at startup and again before every fetch (including each redirect hop):
hosts that are loopback, link-local (where cloud instance-metadata
endpoints live), RFC 1918 private, carrier-grade NAT, IPv6 unique-local,
`localhost`, or reserved-internal names (`metadata`, `*.internal`) are
rejected unless the source sets `allow_private_destinations = true` — a
local-development opt-in for fixture servers. The policy checks the
configured host literally and does not resolve DNS. The same policy applies
to the s3 transport's `endpoint_url`.

#### filesystem

Requires `root`, resolved relative to the config file and canonicalized at
startup. Symlinks below the root are always rejected.

#### s3

Requires `bucket` and `region`; optional `endpoint_url` and
`force_path_style` support local S3-compatible servers.

### S3 credentials and permissions

Credentials are never read from TOML. The adapter uses the standard AWS SDK
credential provider chain: environment variables
(`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`/`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`), shared config/credentials
files and profiles, and instance/task roles.

The service needs `s3:GetObject` on the configured prefix. With `GetObject`
permission alone, S3 answers a missing key with 403 instead of 404 unless
the principal also has `s3:ListBucket`; without list permission every
missing object is reported (correctly, per the error taxonomy) as 502
source-unavailable rather than 404. Grant `s3:ListBucket` on the bucket if
you want missing keys to become cacheable 404s.

Every validation rule is enforced at startup with a specific error. When in
doubt, the startup error messages and `config.example.toml` are
authoritative.

---

Source: https://pixtega.com/docs/api.html

## API reference

The entire API is one endpoint, answering GET and HEAD. Everything else —
method, path shape, transform, version token — is strictly validated, and
every derived image has exactly one URL.

### URL grammar

```text
GET /images/{mount}/{source-path}/{transform}[?v={source-version}]
```

Example:

```text
GET /images/public/photos/example.jpg/w1280.webp?v=7d91c2
```

- `{mount}` selects a configured source. Callers can never supply a
  hostname, bucket, directory, or transport.
- `{source-path}` is everything between the mount and the final segment. It
  is opaque, decoded exactly once, and strictly validated: no traversal, no
  encoded delimiters, canonical percent-encoding only.
- `{transform}` is the final segment: `w{width}[,q{quality}].{format}` with
  `format` one of `webp`, `avif`, `jpeg` (no aliases). Width must be in the
  configured allowlist; quality must be in the selected format's allowlist.
  Omitting `q` uses the format's default; spelling out the default is
  rejected, so each derived image has exactly one URL.
- `v` is an opaque version token (`[A-Za-z0-9._~-]{1,128}`) used only for
  cache policy. The service never appends it to the upstream key. Callers
  must change `v` whenever the source bytes change. The `version_token`
  configuration key can downgrade (`ignore`) or reject (`reject`) it.
- `GET` and `HEAD` are supported; `HEAD` returns exactly the `GET`
  response — same status and headers, including `Content-Length` — with
  the body dropped. Anything else is 405, with an `Allow: GET, HEAD`
  header. Request targets over 8192 bytes are rejected.

The service never upscales: a source narrower than the requested width
keeps its original dimensions.

### Caching

| Response | Cache-Control |
| --- | --- |
| 200 with `v` | `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` |
| 200 without `v` | `public, max-age={unversioned_success_ttl_seconds}` |
| 404 | `public, max-age={not_found_ttl_seconds}` |
| every other error | `no-store` |

Do not enable year-long immutable caching unless every caller changes `v`
when source bytes change; the service cannot verify this for you. The
table shows the default `version_token = "accept"`: with `"ignore"` a 200
with `v` uses the unversioned policy instead, and with `"reject"` any `v`
is a 400.

### Errors

Errors are JSON: `{ "error": "message" }`.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 400 | invalid path, mount, query, transform, width, format, or quality |
| 404 | the source answered authoritatively that the object is absent |
| 405 | method other than GET or HEAD |
| 500 | flatten/encode failed after a valid source was accepted |
| 502 | source answered without a usable object: permission denied, unexpected upstream status, oversized content, undecodable or unsupported image bytes |
| 504 | fetching the source timed out, or the whole request exceeded `request_timeout_ms` |

Permission denial is always 502, never 404, so a misconfigured bucket
cannot be cached as "missing".

### Response headers

Successful responses carry the derived image's `Content-Type` and the
`Cache-Control` policy above. Every response — success or error — also
carries `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`,
`Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'`, and
`X-Frame-Options: DENY`.

### Observability

The service emits one structured JSON completion event per request on
stdout, with status, a stable outcome from a closed set (`success`,
`rejected_request`, `not_found`, `timeout`, `source_too_large`,
`source_unavailable`, `undecodable_source`, `flatten_failed`,
`encode_failed`), mount, output width/format, upstream status, byte counts,
and elapsed milliseconds. Response bodies, credentials, and `v` values are
never logged.

Path validation and adapter behavior are covered further in the README
(https://github.com/kroofy/Pixtega/blob/main/README.md) and pinned down by
the project's test suite.

---

Source: https://pixtega.com/docs/aws-lambda.html

## Deploy on AWS Lambda

The recommended serverless path: a Lambda container image built from
`Dockerfile.lambda`, fronted by a Function URL. The image is the standard
container plus the AWS Lambda Web Adapter extension, which translates
Lambda invocations into plain HTTP — the binary contains no Lambda-specific
code and the same image runs on ECS, EC2, or locally.

### How it fits together

- **`Dockerfile.lambda`** adds the Lambda Web Adapter
  (https://github.com/aws/aws-lambda-web-adapter) as a Lambda extension and
  clears the default command, so configuration comes from the environment
  instead of a baked-in file.
- **Inline configuration.** The service reads its full TOML configuration
  from the `CONFIG` environment variable when no file is given (see
  Configuration above), so config changes are a Lambda environment update,
  never an image rebuild. Keep `listen_address = "0.0.0.0:8080"` — the
  adapter forwards to port 8080 by default.
- **TCP readiness.** The image sets
  `AWS_LWA_READINESS_CHECK_PROTOCOL=tcp` because the service has no HTTP
  health endpoint (`GET /` is a 400 by design); the adapter waits for the
  TCP socket instead of an HTTP 200.
- **Response streaming by default.** The image sets
  `AWS_LWA_INVOKE_MODE=response_stream`, so create the Function URL with
  `--invoke-mode RESPONSE_STREAM` to match. If the two disagree, responses
  come back as the adapter's buffered JSON envelope instead of image bytes.
  ALB cannot stream — behind an ALB, override the function environment to
  `AWS_LWA_INVOKE_MODE=buffered`. API Gateway streams only when the REST
  proxy integration uses `responseTransferMode=STREAM` with a
  `/response-streaming-invocations` integration URI; otherwise override
  to buffered so the modes match.
- **S3 sources use the execution role.** Credentials are never read from
  TOML; grant the function's role `s3:GetObject` on the configured prefix
  (and ideally `s3:ListBucket` so missing keys become cacheable 404s
  instead of 502s).

### Deployment outline

```bash
# 1. Build the Lambda image
docker build -f Dockerfile.lambda --platform linux/amd64 -t pixtega-lambda .

# 2. Push to ECR
docker tag pixtega-lambda "$ECR_REPO:latest"
docker push "$ECR_REPO:latest"

# 3. Create the function with inline TOML configuration
aws lambda create-function \
  --function-name pixtega \
  --package-type Image \
  --code ImageUri="$ECR_REPO:latest" \
  --role "$ROLE_ARN" \
  --memory-size 1024 --timeout 30 \
  --environment "Variables={CONFIG=$(cat deploy/lambda/example-config.toml)}"

# 4. Expose a Function URL for a smoke test (dev only — see below)
aws lambda create-function-url-config --function-name pixtega \
  --auth-type NONE --invoke-mode RESPONSE_STREAM
curl -o out.webp "${FUNCTION_URL}images/fixtures/photos/example.jpg/w640.webp"
```

The complete walkthrough — ECR login, IAM policies, permissions for the
public URL, and the smoke test — lives in the repository at
https://github.com/kroofy/Pixtega/blob/main/deploy/lambda/README.md, with a
ready-made example-config.toml
(https://github.com/kroofy/Pixtega/blob/main/deploy/lambda/example-config.toml).

### Production exposure

`--auth-type NONE` makes the Function URL publicly invokable by anyone,
with no cache absorbing traffic and no auth layer — it is for the smoke
test above only, not for an internet-facing production endpoint. For
production, put CloudFront in front (the service's cache policy is designed
for it), switch the Function URL to `--auth-type AWS_IAM` with a CloudFront
Origin Access Control (OAC) for Lambda Function URLs so only the
distribution can invoke the function, and remove the public `NONE` invoke
permission. Details in
https://github.com/kroofy/Pixtega/blob/main/deploy/lambda/README.md.

### Caveats

- **6 MB response limit.** Buffered Function URL responses are capped at
  about 6 MB, so the image and this guide default to response streaming
  (`AWS_LWA_INVOKE_MODE=response_stream` in the image plus
  `--invoke-mode RESPONSE_STREAM` on the Function URL), which raises the
  limit substantially. The two must stay in sync. To run buffered instead,
  set the Function URL to BUFFERED *and* `AWS_LWA_INVOKE_MODE=buffered` on
  the function, and consider constraining `allowed_widths` and
  `allowed_qualities` so oversized outputs cannot be produced. Buffered is
  required where Function URL streaming is unavailable: VPC-attached
  functions and some AWS Regions.
- **Cold starts.** Each new execution environment loads libvips, validates
  configuration, and verifies every enabled encoder, so the first request
  is noticeably slower than warm ones. A CDN in front absorbs most of this
  — the service's cache policy is designed for exactly that.
- **Environment size.** Lambda caps the function environment at 4 KB total.
  If your TOML does not fit in `CONFIG`, bake a config file into the image
  and point `CONFIG_FILE` at it.

Prefer a plain container platform? The standard `Dockerfile` image works
unchanged on ECS, Fargate, or any Docker host — see Getting started above.

---

Source: https://github.com/kroofy/Pixtega/blob/main/README.md

## Clients and packages

- **Rust**: the crate and binary are named `pixtega`
  (https://crates.io/crates/pixtega). Source:
  https://github.com/kroofy/Pixtega.
- **JavaScript**: pure URL builders (`pixtegaUrl`, `pixtegaSrcSet`,
  `pixtegaPicture`) for this service's URL contract live in the
  repository's `js/` directory, published to npm from each release tag
  as `pixtega` (https://www.npmjs.com/package/pixtega) and
  `@pixtega/url` (https://www.npmjs.com/package/@pixtega/url) — the
  scoped package is a thin re-export with the same API. Install with
  `npm install pixtega` or `npm install @pixtega/url`.

The client builds strings and never fetches. It rejects everything the
server's fixed URL grammar rejects (segment encoding, transform shape, the
`v` token alphabet), but it cannot know your server's configured width and
quality allowlists. A URL this client accepts can still get a 400: a width
or quality outside the allowlist, or an explicit quality equal to the
format's default (omit `quality` to use the default).

```js
import { pixtegaUrl, pixtegaSrcSet, pixtegaPicture } from "pixtega";

pixtegaUrl({
  base: "https://images.example.com",
  mount: "public",
  path: "photos/example.jpg", // decoded; also accepts ["photos", "example.jpg"]
  width: 1280,
  format: "webp", // "webp" | "avif" | "jpeg"
  quality: 85,    // optional; must be allowlisted and not the default
  v: "7d91c2",    // optional version token for immutable caching
  pathPrefix: "/images", // default
});
// => "https://images.example.com/images/public/photos/example.jpg/w1280,q85.webp?v=7d91c2"

pixtegaSrcSet({ base, mount, path, format: "webp", widths: [640, 1280] });
// => ".../w640.webp 640w, .../w1280.webp 1280w"

pixtegaPicture({ base, mount, path, widths: [640, 1280], formats: ["avif", "webp", "jpeg"] });
// => { sources: [{ type: "image/avif", srcset }, ...],
//      img: { src: ".../w1280.jpeg" } }
```

`pixtegaPicture` lists `sources` in the order given (browsers pick the
first supported type) and uses the last format for the fallback `img.src`,
so put the most widely supported format last.
